raw_case_text: A 28-year-old woman, pregnant, black, housekeeper, from Sao Francisco do Itabapoana, RJ, was admitted to the hospital on June 29th 2016, presenting weakness in the lower limbs and a consequent inability to ambulate for the previous week. The patient affirmed not having experienced similar episodes previously and claimed to be free of comorbidities. The patient reported rash on her limbs, pruritus and vomiting approximately 1 month before admission to the hospital. Initial obstetric examinations showed globular abdomen, unlimited uterus and absence of vaginal bleeding. The fetal heartbeat was not detected in the Sonar Doppler. Transvaginal ultrasonography evidenced a single fetus with longitudinal status and cephalic circumference suggesting 15 weeks of gestational age, normohydramnios, lack of heartbeat, and non-apparent active movements, which lead to the diagnosis of death and retained fetus (stillbirth). The patient was admitted to curettage and remained in hospital for 30 days. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture and exams of the patient's peripheral blood revealed normal parameters (Table S1). The IgM serology for Dengue, Chikungunya, Zika, Epstein Barr and Cytomegalovirus were non-reactive (in further sections of this paper, diagnosis of ZIKV infection was confirmed by specific staining in placental and fetal tissues). The patient evolved to ascending and symmetrical flaccid tetraparesis, paresthesia, areflexia, presenting hands with pendular movement, dysautonomia (resting tachycardia and hypertension) and signs of respiratory insufficiency (mild dyspnea at rest which worsens upon effort), characterizing the GBS. The patient was further treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (30 g/day) for five days, atenolol 50 mg 12/12 h, amlodipine 5 mg 24 h, motor rehabilitation, respiratory physiotherapy and psychological intervention. In the second week of disease evolution, the neurological examination showed symmetric flaccid tetraparesis, motor incoordination, global areflexia and sensitive disorders (tactile and thermal distal hypoesthesia). Neurological follow up during and after the hospitalization period are described in Table S2. During the fourth week of disease progress, the patient was admitted to electroneuromyography, which revealed peripheral, acquired, chronic, symmetrical, diffuse, myelin and axonal (predominantly myelin), sensory and motor polyneuropathy: a condition that affected the peripheral nerves of the upper and lower limbs. In addition to that, the patient showed signs of neurogenic myopathy and muscular denervation. Together, these findings were compatible with polyradiculoneuropathy. By the end of the fourth week, the patient was discharged from the hospital under prescription of antihypertensive drugs and still being followed up by motor physical therapy. After 40 days of hospital discharge, the patient was orthostatic, walking-dependent for small distances and with pain sequels in the lower limbs. Five months later, residual sequels were still present with autonomous difficult scarvant gait. After 12 months, the gait patterns were regular; however, the speed and execution of upward and downward movements remained affected. Finally, the patient returned to her daily activities. Methods performed in this work using the placenta and fetal organs are described in Supplementary Material.

subjective.chief_complaint: 28-year-old pregnant female presenting with lower extremity weakness and inability to ambulate for 1 week.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Approximately 1 month prior to hospital admission, the patient experienced a pruritic rash on her limbs and vomiting. One week prior to admission, she developed progressive lower extremity weakness that left her unable to walk. Upon admission on June 29, 2016, intrauterine fetal demise was diagnosed and she underwent uterine curettage. Following the procedure, her neurological symptoms progressed to ascending symmetrical flaccid tetraparesis, paresthesias, areflexia, pendular hand movements, autonomic instability (resting tachycardia and hypertension), and respiratory insufficiency with exertional dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior neurological episodes; no chronic comorbidities; residence in São Francisco de Itabapoana, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; pregnant housekeeper.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pruritus, vomiting, paresthesias, mild resting dyspnea worsening on effort; denies vaginal bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Obstetric: Globular abdomen, gravid uterus, absence of vaginal bleeding; fetal heart tones absent by Doppler. Neurological (admission/week 2): Symmetrical flaccid tetraparesis, global areflexia, pendular hand movements, motor incoordination, distal tactile and thermal hypoesthesia, resting tachycardia, and hypertension.
objective.routine_investigations: Peripheral blood laboratory examinations revealed normal parameters. Transvaginal ultrasonography: Single fetus in longitudinal lie with cephalic circumference consistent with 15 weeks gestational age, normohydramnios, absent cardiac activity, and absent active movements, confirming intrauterine fetal death.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cytochemical parameters. Electroneuromyography (week 4): Peripheral, acquired, symmetrical, diffuse, predominantly demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy involving the upper and lower extremities, with signs of neurogenic myopathy and muscular denervation, compatible with acute polyradiculoneuropathy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy) and intrauterine fetal demise associated with Zika virus infection. Serum IgM serologies for Zika virus, dengue virus, chikungunya virus, Epstein-Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were non-reactive; definitive diagnosis was confirmed by specific histochemical/immunohistochemical staining for ZIKV in placental and fetal tissues. Treatment included uterine curettage, intravenous immunoglobulin (30 g/day for 5 days), atenolol (50 mg every 12 hours), amlodipine (5 mg daily), respiratory physiotherapy, and motor rehabilitation. By 40 days post-discharge she was able to stand and ambulate short distances with assistance; at 5 months she walked with a steppage gait; and by 12 months achieved regular gait pattern with residual speed limitations and returned to daily activities.
